gbs333-aa7793-d1e107.summary: States the question: whether practical and speculative knowledge are distinguished by ends or by objects.

gbs333-aa7793-d1e127.summary: First notandum distinguishing praxis from practical knowledge (practical act): practical knowledge is actual or habitual adhesive knowledge of a practical proposition, while praxis is the operation in our power signified by the practical proposition or its part. Assent to 'alms are to be given to the needy' is practical knowledge; giving alms is praxis. Likewise assent to 'a syllogism must be formed in mode and figure' is practical knowledge; forming the syllogism is praxis.
claims: Practical knowledge is adhesive knowledge of a practical proposition.
Praxis is the operation in our power that the practical proposition signifies.
Practical knowledge and praxis are distinct.

gbs333-aa7793-d1e167.summary: Offers a first definition: practical knowledge is knowledge of a true complex that shows or dictates, universally or particularly, free operation. Examples: 'God is to be loved with the whole soul', 'God is to be worshipped with latria', 'seek first the kingdom of God', 'with the heart one believes unto justice, with the mouth confession is made unto salvation', 'marble must be cut with iron, earth with the plough'. Knowledge of these propositions is practical; the operations they signify are praxes.
claims: Practical knowledge is knowledge of a true complex that shows or dictates free operation.
Both moral-religious precepts and technical rules count as practical knowledge.

gbs333-aa7793-d1e198.summary: Raises an objection: on that definition, propositions such as 'contrary is destroyed by contrary', 'like is fostered by like', 'habit is generated from acts', 'hay multiplies on watered land' would not be practical. But this is false, since they are ordered to work, concern objects operable by us, and direct operation (e.g. whoever wishes to destroy a quality should apply its contrary).
claims: (Objection) General natural truths that guide action, such as 'contrary destroys contrary', seem practical but fall outside the first definition.

gbs333-aa7793-d1e222.summary: In response proposes a refined definition: practical knowledge is adhesive knowledge of a true complex directive of a work in our power more than incomplex knowledge is. It is 'directive' because its possessor can know whether, when, why, where, or how to act. The 'more than incomplex knowledge' clause excludes propositions like 'love is a quality of the mind', 'God is infinitely good', 'stone is hard', 'water is fluid', which are simply speculative even though they can somewhat direct action (God's infinite goodness directs us to love him maximally; stone's hardness guides the mason's tools), because they direct no more than distinct incomplex knowledge of their terms; otherwise all knowledge would be practical. For a complex to be directive, it or one of its terms must signify a free operation, actively or passively, formally or equivalently, since praxis is always a partial object of practical knowledge. Speculative knowledge is defined oppositely.
claims: Practical knowledge is adhesive knowledge of a true complex that directs a work in our power more than incomplex knowledge does.
Directive knowledge informs whether, when, why, where, or how to act.
Propositions like 'God is infinitely good' or 'stone is hard' are speculative though indirectly guiding.
A practical complex must signify, formally or equivalently, a free operation; praxis is always a partial object of practical knowledge.
Speculative knowledge is defined by opposition.

gbs333-aa7793-d1e290.summary: Second notandum: some distinguish the end of the knower (to which the knower orders the science) from the end of the science, which is twofold: the per se and principal end to which the science is by nature ordered, and the accidental or secondary end, which depends on the knower's intention. They hold that practical and speculative science differ by their per se principal end, work for the one and truth for the other.
claims: (Reported view) Practical and speculative sciences are distinguished by their per se ends: work vs. truth.
(Reported view) The end of the science differs from the end of the knower.

gbs333-aa7793-d1e319.summary: Against this, Ockham argues that the end of the science is the same as the end of the knower and that the same end can belong to speculative and practical science. He distinguishes two senses of end: the end acquired by an operation, loved with love of concupiscence (as health is the end of walking), first in intention but last in execution, really an effect and usually less noble than that for which it is sought, called the finis quo; and the end loved with love of friendship for whose sake the first is produced (oneself, or God for one who loves God above all), which often pre-exists the operation, is not an effect, is not acquired by it, and is not less noble, called the finis gratia cuius.
claims: The end of a science is the same as the end of the knower.
The same end can belong to speculative and practical sciences.
The finis quo is loved with concupiscence, is an effect of the operation, and is usually less noble.
The finis gratia cuius is loved with friendship, often pre-exists the operation, and is not its effect.
concepts: finis quo vs. finis gratia cuius

gbs333-aa7793-d1e387.summary: Third notandum: the end of a science properly speaking is what the learner loves, with friendship or concupiscence, that moves him to acquire the science; simply speaking it is the same as what is intended and loved by the knower as final cause of the science, but not as cause of the knower. Example: one who out of self-love desires science for gain: he himself, loved with love of friendship, is a cause of the science (since from him so loved the science proceeds), though not cause of himself; the desired gain is also in some way the final cause of the science, though neither gain nor love of gain causes the knower, who does not depend on it.
claims: The end of a science is what the learner loves and what moves him to acquire it.
That end is the final cause of the science, not of the knower.
Both the self loved in friendship and the gain desired can be final causes of the science.
concepts: end of the science = end of the knower

gbs333-aa7793-d1e436.summary: Fourth notandum: 'to be distinguished by something' has many senses: by intrinsic or extrinsic factors; by causes of their distinction, whether limited and proper or unlimited and common; or by things proper to them, such as properties, proper subjects, or proper effects.
claims: Being distinguished 'by' something may mean intrinsically, extrinsically, causally (by proper or common causes), or by proper features (properties, subjects, effects).

gbs333-aa7793-d1e458.summary: Rubric marking the second article, which contains the conclusions.

gbs333-aa7793-d1e463.summary: First conclusion: practical and speculative sciences are distinguished intrinsically and formally by themselves and not by anything else, since sciences are simple forms and simple forms can be formally distinguished only by themselves.
claims: Practical and speculative sciences are formally distinguished by themselves.
Sciences are simple forms.
Simple forms are formally distinct only by themselves.

gbs333-aa7793-d1e479.summary: Second and third conclusions. Second: practical and speculative sciences are distinguished causally by their end or ends, just as they are by efficient causes, since a thing has distinct being from that from which it has being, and it has being from its final as from its efficient cause; even two sciences with the same final cause are causally distinguished by it, just as all creatures are causally distinguished by God, the cause of their distinction. Third: they are not distinguished by subjects of attribution, since there can be speculative and practical sciences of the same subject: any subject with some attributes signifying what is in our power and others signifying what is not can be the subject of both practical and speculative conclusions.
claims: Practical and speculative sciences are distinguished causally by ends, as by efficient causes.
Even a common final cause distinguishes sciences causally, as God distinguishes all creatures.
Practical and speculative sciences are not distinguished by their subjects of attribution.
The same subject can be the subject of practical and speculative conclusions.

gbs333-aa7793-d1e538.summary: Fourth conclusion: practical and speculative science are distinguished by their objects, i.e., known conclusions, as by things proper to them, since the same conclusion cannot be the object of both: either it directs praxis, and its science is practical, or it does not, and its science is speculative.
claims: Practical and speculative sciences are distinguished by their objects (known conclusions) as proper to them.
No conclusion can be both practically and speculatively known.

gbs333-aa7793-d1e560.summary: Fifth conclusion: taking 'end' improperly, as the doctors commonly do, for what ought by right reason to be intended by one acquiring the science, practical and speculative sciences are distinguished by ends as proper to them: work or operating for the practical, consideration for the speculative. From this, practical science is defined as science directive of some praxis, i.e., science of a conclusion directing the knower regarding a work or operation in the power of our will.
claims: Taking 'end' improperly as the right-reason end of acquisition, practical and speculative sciences differ by ends: operation vs. consideration.
Practical science is science of a conclusion directing the knower about a work in the will's power.

gbs333-aa7793-d1e596.summary: Distinguishes two ways practical conclusions direct voluntary operation: dictatively, by determinately signifying that something is to be done ('God is to be worshipped with latria on the Sabbath', 'the church is to be repaired'); and ostensively, by showing the way of operating by which one can act rightly according to the norm of art, not necessarily of virtue ('a house is composed of foundation, walls, and roof', 'timber must be hewn thus'). The first belongs to prudence, which knows when and under what circumstances to act so that the work is virtuous; the second to the mechanical arts and the practical liberal arts (logic, grammar, rhetoric), which teach how to argue, speak congruently, or persuade, but not when, where, before whom, or for what end.
claims: Practical conclusions direct either dictatively (what must be done) or ostensively (how to do it).
Dictative direction belongs to prudence.
Ostensive direction belongs to mechanical arts and the practical liberal arts (logic, grammar, rhetoric).
Arts teach how to act but not when, where, or for what end.
concepts: logic, grammar, rhetoric as practical arts
norm of art vs. norm of virtue

gbs333-aa7793-d1e685.summary: Third article, on the difference between prudence and moral philosophy, citing Ockham's Quodlibet IV q. 6 and Book III q. 12 (and Biel's own III d. 36). Prudence can be a simple habit dictating about an agibile according to right reason, or an aggregate of such habits required for living well. As a simple habit it has three senses: (1) generally, any habit directive of any agibile, whether a self-evident proposition, one known by experience, or one deduced by teaching (e.g. 'every benefactor should be benefited'; 'the irate are to be soothed with gentle words'); (2) a habit immediately directive about a particular agibile through a particular proposition evidently deduced from a self-evident one ('this benefactor should be benefited'); (3) most strictly, a habit immediately directive about a particular agibile received through experience alone, not deduced from universals ('this irate man is to be soothed with gentle words').
claims: Prudence may be taken as a simple habit or as an aggregate of habits.
As a simple habit, prudence has three senses: any directive habit; a particular directive habit deduced from self-evident principles; a particular directive habit acquired by experience alone.

gbs333-aa7793-d1e785.summary: Defines the habit of moral philosophy or moral science: a habit directive about action acquired by teaching from self-evident principles or experience, not from acts about particulars.
claims: Moral science is a directive habit acquired by teaching from self-evident principles or experience, not from particular acts.

gbs333-aa7793-d1e796.summary: Applies the distinctions: prudence in the first or second sense does not differ from moral science, since knowledge about a particular agibile insofar as it is deduced doctrinally from self-evident principles belongs to moral science. In the third sense prudence is distinct, since moral science is had by doctrinal deduction and prudence only by experience. This is Aristotle's sense in Ethics VI, where prudence is knowledge of particulars or universals gained solely through experiential acts about singulars, and where he distinguishes prudence from art (as action from making) and from science.
claims: Prudence in the first and second senses does not differ from moral science.
Prudence in the strictest sense differs from moral science as experiential vs. doctrinal knowledge.
Aristotle's distinction of prudence from moral science, art, and science uses this strictest sense.

gbs333-aa7793-d1e857.summary: Summarizes: the distinction between prudence and moral science is proportional to that between experiential knowledge and art, as Aristotle teaches in Ethics VI and the proem of the Metaphysics: from sensation comes memory, from memory experience, and from many experiences a universal that is the principle of art. Biel glosses in Ockhamist terms: sensation is intuitive knowledge; memory is abstractive knowledge of the same object; both are simple singular apprehensive cognitions; and from many memories comes experience.
claims: Prudence relates to moral science as experience to art.
Sensation (intuitive) gives rise to memory (abstractive), memory to experience, experience to universal principles of art.
Sensation and memory are simple, singular, apprehensive cognitions.

gbs333-aa7793-d1e896.summary: Defines experience (experimentum): a judgment about a sensed singular caused by many memories of similar previously sensed things. One who has felt this and that fire heat, on seeing another fire he does not touch, judges from memories that it too heats; this judgment is an experience. Experience is thus judicative knowledge of a singular from memories of similar singulars.
claims: Experience is a judgment about a singular caused by many memories of similar previously sensed singulars.

gbs333-aa7793-d1e928.summary: Recapitulates: sensation is the first intuitive knowledge, memory is abstractive, experience is adhesive or judicative; from many experiences a universal is gathered (as described in Prologue q. 2), which is a principle of art.
claims: Sensation is intuitive, memory abstractive, experience adhesive or judicative.
Universal principles of art are gathered from many experiences.

gbs333-aa7793-d1e946.summary: Contrasts the expert and the artisan: the expert proceeds from singulars, from which he gathers many universals known to him by experience, but as such does not acquire universals from more universal ones; the artisan as such begins from self-evident principles or principles known by experience, if not his own then believed from others who have experienced them.
claims: The expert gathers universals from singulars by experience.
The artisan begins from self-evident principles or from experiential principles, possibly believed from others.

gbs333-aa7793-d1e968.summary: Corollary: the pure artisan who is not also experienced has science only of conclusions deduced mediately or immediately from self-evident principles, not of those deduced from experiential principles he did not himself acquire, of which he lacks evident knowledge. The same holds of prudence and moral science: the prudent man is like the expert, the moral scientist like the artisan. Prudence taken aggregatively can likewise be taken in three ways, as an aggregate of simple prudences in each of the three senses, with proportionate conclusions.
claims: A pure artisan without experience has evident science only of conclusions from self-evident principles.
Conclusions from experiential principles believed on others' testimony are not evidently known.
The prudent person is as the expert; the moral scientist as the artisan.
Aggregate prudence admits the same threefold distinction.

gbs333-aa7793.summary: Quaestio 11 asks whether practical and speculative knowledge are distinguished by ends or by objects. Biel first separates practical knowledge (assent to a practical proposition) from praxis (the free operation it signifies). He refines a definition through an objection: practical knowledge is adhesive knowledge of a true complex that directs a work in our power more than incomplex knowledge of its terms does, so that praxis is always a partial object. Against those who distinguish the per se end of a science from the knower's end, he argues with Ockham that the two coincide. He distinguishes the finis quo, loved with concupiscence and an effect of the act, from the finis gratia cuius, loved with friendship. Five conclusions follow. Practical and speculative sciences are formally distinguished by themselves, as simple forms, and causally by their ends. They are not distinguished by subjects of attribution, since one subject can bear both kinds of conclusion. They are properly distinguished by their objects (known conclusions, directive of praxis or not), and by ends only in the improper sense of what right reason intends (operation vs. consideration). Practical direction is dictative, belonging to prudence, or ostensive, belonging to the mechanical and practical liberal arts. A third article distinguishes prudence from moral philosophy. Prudence in its strictest sense is directive knowledge of particulars gained by experience alone, differing from doctrinally acquired moral science as experience differs from art. This is grounded in an Ockhamist reading of Aristotle's sequence of sensation (intuitive), memory (abstractive), experience (judicative), and universal principle, and in the contrast between the expert and the pure artisan.
claims: Practical knowledge is assent to a complex that directs a free operation more than knowledge of its terms does; praxis is always its partial object.
Practical and speculative sciences are distinguished formally by themselves, causally by ends, and properly by their objects, not by their subjects.
The end of a science is the same as the end of the knower.
Practical direction is either dictative (prudence) or ostensive (arts).
Prudence in the strictest sense differs from moral science as experiential from doctrinal knowledge.
concepts: finis quo vs. finis gratia cuius
